codex.worst_flaw: The record-only audit leaves a launch-blocking safety risk because technicians can earn credit for clearing hazardous jobs without actually checking for hazards.

claude.worst_flaw: Auditing only 10 records a week gives a weak check for rushed or falsified hazard answers across 300 technicians, and nothing in the design records policy or event versions or checks the credit counts against an independent shadow tally.

holistic.reason: Union-involved co-design, paid-time reward, hold-equals-credit and private counts make it approvable, but a one-hour reward over two weeks is modest, monitoring is heavy, and lasting change depends on the app fixes rather than the incentive.

codex.worst_flaw: The audit lacks an independent check that technicians identified hazards and placed jobs on hold when required, leaving a launch-blocking risk that the programme rewards unsafe clearances.

claude.worst_flaw: The 80% target is the same for everyone regardless of job volume or case mix, and the two-wave comparison only spans two weeks with no stated sample size, uncertainty handling or cost and harm thresholds, so nothing isolates whether the reward adds meaningful value over plain support.

holistic.reason: Union co-design, workflow fixes first, a once-only reward with fair counting rules, protected stop-work authority and clear sampling and pause triggers make it approvable, though the 30-minute reward is modest and the verification and dispute process is heavy for a 300-person firm.

claude.worst_flaw: Learning and audit are thin: a two-week stagger compares halves of crews with no handling of spillover or case mix, no uncertainty or minimum sample, and no harm or cost thresholds; there are also no replayable event or policy versions and no independent shadow validation of the counts, and a 10-record weekly sample across 300 technicians is too small to detect rushed or backdated checklists reliably.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch is blocked because the audit relies on job records and lacks an independent check for fabricated safety answers or work that proceeds despite a required hold.

holistic.reason: Union co-design, privacy protections, safety-hold parity, audit sampling and a stagger-based test make it approvable, but a one-hour reward and two-week window are modest and the exit plan relies on workflow fixes more than the incentive.

claude.worst_flaw: The staggered squad comparison has no predefined sample size, uncertainty handling or cost and harm outcomes, and it ignores spillover from shared reviewers across squads. A 25-person team cannot reliably isolate what the reward adds that way, and the team-wide weekly on-time percentage plus the individual PTO target still leave room for social pressure, with no check on morale or cooperation.

codex.worst_flaw: Launch should wait because timestamps establish when reviews were submitted, and the design gives no method for using the quality sample to validate or correct the qualifying-review rate that determines success.

holistic.reason: Fixing the queue first, privacy-respecting small rewards and a built-in test of whether the reward adds anything suit sceptical engineers, but the many rules, sampling and calendar logic are heavy to run, and a one-hour time-off prize may barely register.

codex.worst_flaw: The two waves share a review queue and can cover each other’s PRs, so the comparison could mistake a shift in who gets credit for an improvement caused by the reward.

claude.worst_flaw: The wave comparison of about 12 engineers each over two weeks has no stated sample size, uncertainty handling, or spillover control (both waves share PRs and reviewers), so the 80% decision rule could be driven by noise, and nothing records event or policy versions for replaying the counts.

holistic.reason: Well-designed, fair and low-surveillance with workflow fixes and an hour of paid time off that sceptical engineers should accept, but it is administratively heavy, the incentive is small, and the lasting effect depends on whether the protected slots and backup reviewers persist.

claude.worst_flaw: The learning design is weak: it compares two rotations of about 12 engineers each over two weeks, the shared queue lets each rotation affect the other, there is no power or uncertainty plan, and the 80% decision threshold is not tied to a measured counterfactual, so the incentive's added value over plain queue support stays unisolated.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot compares two rotations sharing a queue without accounting for their baseline performance, case mix, or spillovers, so it cannot reliably isolate the reward’s effect.

holistic.reason: Fixing the queue first, using a private reward and measuring the result against a decision rule suit sceptical engineers, but the rules are dense (clock edge cases, credit clawbacks, per-person windows), and a one-hour reward is small and may be seen as complicated or as a way to monitor people.

codex.worst_flaw: A ward’s entire two-week reward window can pass between monthly audits, leaving Infection Prevention without timely evidence to detect a drop in hand-hygiene compliance and pause rewards.

claude.worst_flaw: The reward pays for one demonstrated entry. The measure of 'accurate kiosk capture' depends on matching observed opportunities to kiosk entries by ward, time window and moment type without nurse identity. Matches can be ambiguous, and nothing tests whether routine logging fills the kiosk with invented or retrospective entries, so the core adoption measure may not be valid.

holistic.reason: Rewarding a verified, accurate entry with release time and independent audit safeguards, harm pauses and a pre-set 4-week decision rule is a well-controlled pilot, but a one-time reward and heavy operational complexity limit adoption and the durability of the habit after rewards end.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot can retain the kiosk even if nurses record only one moment per shift, because it never measures what share of eligible hand-hygiene moments they log.

claude.worst_flaw: Kiosk logging is the stated goal, yet no valid kiosk-capture measure exists and the plan never reconciles uptake with audited compliance. It also has no event history or staffed appeal route, and with only three wards and monthly audits that are prone to Hawthorne effects, the rotating comparison is too underpowered to isolate what recognition adds.

holistic.reason: Well-designed pilot with safe measurement, staggered rollout, protected time and audited outcomes, but the reward is only verbal thanks from the director and the kiosk is mostly visible through huddle boards, so motivation and post-incentive persistence are modest.

claude.worst_flaw: The main adoption measure counts any shift with at least one saved kiosk entry, so it never checks whether the logged moments match the real hand-hygiene opportunities. That leaves the kiosk data largely detached from the behaviour the hospital actually cares about, which is observed compliance.

codex.worst_flaw: A single saved entry gives a shift full adoption credit, so the post-reward evaluation cannot tell what share of eligible hand-hygiene moments nurses actually log.

holistic.reason: Well-designed, safety-conscious pilot with independent audit, privacy protections and a staggered rollout, but a one-time break for a single entry is a weak, brief incentive that may not sustain logging, and the logged adoption measure is only loosely tied to actual hand-hygiene compliance.

codex.worst_flaw: The sole success metric can clear the retention threshold through valid exceptions alone, leaving the programme without evidence that useful article linking or publication increased.

claude.worst_flaw: The weekly audit samples only 12 credited tickets, so it cannot detect displacement into uncredited work. It also has no independent check on whether articles are relevant or whether exceptions are valid, and the 3-of-12 pause threshold is noisy. Meanwhile the existing CSAT bonus could still push agents to rush closures, and the design does not reconcile that pressure.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with pilot feedback, fraud checks, private feedback, a stagger to test lift, and a metric redefined to include valid exceptions, but it is complex for a 60-person org, relies on a weekly manual audit, and the lasting effect rests on the default form change rather than on the one-hour reward.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot has a launch blocker because recording more valid exceptions can earn rewards and meet the success threshold without any increase in article linking or writing.

claude.worst_flaw: The design does not set the existing CSAT bonus against the new knowledge-base goal, so it never checks whether a shift in ticket mix or delayed replies would change bonus pay. Its learning design also has no estimate of the effect size the cohorts can detect and no rule for what happens to credit when a submitted draft is later rejected in review.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with verification, quality sampling, staggered rollout and a pre-set decision rule, but the reward is a single paid hour for a short two-week window, and its complexity (three cohorts, exception paths, weekly audits) could dilute salience and rely on workflow defaults rather than intrinsic motivation to sustain behaviour after prizes end.

codex.worst_flaw: The design sets a pause rule for QA failures but no threshold for pausing rewards if customer satisfaction falls or resolution times rise.

claude.worst_flaw: The flat 70% two-week target jumps from a 12% baseline without being tied to measured feasibility or case mix, and it ignores agents with zero resolved tickets, so the all-or-nothing threshold can be unfair and push people toward loosely relevant links or overused exceptions, which a 10-ticket weekly audit across 60 agents is too thin to catch reliably.

holistic.reason: Unusually thorough on measurement, exception handling, gaming safeguards and fixing the workflow first, but a one-paid-hour reward for a 70% bar is small, the design is complex for a 60-person team, and relying on a default-first prompt plus 30-minute practice for durability is plausible but unproven.
